rv.q: “The Lonely Few,” the achingly romantic, softly sexy, genuinely rocking new musical by Rachel Bonds (“Jonah”) and Zoe Sarnak at MCC Theater, is Lila and Amy’s love story.
Ms. Patten anchors the show, both emotionally and musically, with her moving performance as Lila, whose eyes can seem like searchlights scanning the horizon for signs of a promising future.
Watching these two women make beautiful music together is heart-melting.
The Lonely Few is a fun, feel-good extravaganza that amplifies queer voices and offers electrifying opportunities to feel represented, celebrated, and included.
There is so much talent and charisma flowing off Patten and Iman Jones for you not to be caught up in their messy, passionate love story.
It will be the only thing I listen to for weeks.
This production’s abundance of talent and heart will at least hold your attention.
It’s an admirable collection of songs in search of significance.
If you like rock and romance, don't miss this show.
But we’re seeing—and hearing—only glimmers of it onstage at MCC Theater.
The most frustrating thing about The Lonely Few, though, is the momentary glimpses it offers of a richer, more distinctive show.

There is clarity and compassion in this rock musical that is getting its NYC premiere off-Broadway at MCC Theatre with some compelling back stories and attachment figures that make The Lonely Few even more powerful and electric than the performances and their songs.
The score, by Zoe Sarnak, hits the mark with a mix of angsty up-tempo bangers and misty, heartfelt ballads.
There’s a bracing novelty at the heart of The Lonely Few — a lesbian love affair set to a foot-stomping beat — and Patten and Jones deliver on both the romance and the rebellious rock sound.
"The Lonely Few" is a reminder of how much good entertainment there is Off-Broadway.

The Lonely Few delivered an incredible night that celebrated queer women being able to have the same kind of love stories that everyone else does without the story containing over bigotry or pain beyond the loneliness of being queer and occasionally feeling stuck.
“The Lonely Few” does not offer anything groundbreaking as far as musical theater but it is an enjoyable evening of entertainment with a heartfelt message.

The Lonely Few absolutely deserves the time and attention and is a fantastic choice especially if you are in the market for a new and creative musical that incorporates immersive techniques and is coupled with a fabulous score.

cn.t: This rock musical about a queer love story in small-town Kentucky earns praise for its powerful performances, especially Lauren Patten's vocals, and immersive staging, though critics find the plot predictable and overstuffed with songs.

vr.q: The score by Zoe Sarnak is one of my favorite new scores I've heard in awhile and the performances by this small but mighty cast are fantastic.
That shell is still very entertaining, and there's still a lot to love.
